Test each feature group for a difference between two levels

Source: R/cellpaintr.R
calculateStats.Rd

Average the leave-one-out prediction scores of predictLOO per patient and level, and test in each feature group whether the interest level has higher scores than the reference level.

Usage

calculateStats(
  sce,
  target,
  group,
  assay_type = "tfmfeatures",
  method = c("permutation", "t"),
  n_permutations = 999
)

Arguments

sce

Output of predictLOO

target

Name of target variable for prediction

group

Grouping variable for cross-validation, e.g., patient

assay_type

A string specifying the assay

method

Either `"permutation"` (default) for a permutation test that relabels whole patients, or `"t"` for p-values from the t-distribution

n_permutations

Largest number of relabelings besides the observed labels; if there are more, this many are drawn at random

Value

data.frame with one row per feature group and the columns `Target` (interest level), `Feature` (feature group), `pvalue`, and `log2FoldChange` (log2 ratio of the mean scores of the interest and the reference level). With the permutation test, the attribute `relabelings` holds the number of relabelings, the observed one included.

Details

The test statistic is the one-sided t-statistic for higher mean scores in the interest level. It is paired if every patient (`group`) has cells of both levels, and uses a pooled variance if every patient has cells of one level.

With `method = "permutation"` (the default), the p-value comes from relabeling whole patients: in a paired design, the two levels of a patient are swapped; in an unpaired design, the levels are permuted across patients. For each relabeling, all leave-one-out models are refitted with the settings of the call to predictLOO, and the p-value is the proportion of relabelings, the observed one included, with a statistic at least as large. If there are at most `n_permutations + 1` relabelings (\(2^n\) for \(n\) patients in a paired design), all of them are enumerated and the test is exact; otherwise, `n_permutations` relabelings are drawn at random. The smallest attainable p-value is one over the number of relabelings. Because all models are refitted for every relabeling, the test takes that many times longer than predictLOO. Use set.seed for reproducible results.

With `method = "t"`, the p-value comes from the t-distribution. This is fast but anti-conservative, because the models of different held-out patients share most of their training data, which makes the scores of different patients positively correlated.

Examples

set.seed(23)
cell_file <- generate_data()
sce <- loadData(cell_file)
sce <- transformScale(sce)

sce$Drug <- as.factor(sce$Drug)
sce$Drug <- relevel(sce$Drug, ref = "D1")

sce_single <- predictLOO(
    sce,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    interest_level = "D7", reference_level = "D1",
    n_threads = 1
)

# permutation test; by default, it enumerates all 64 relabelings of the
# six patients, here 9 random relabelings keep the example fast
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    n_permutations = 9
)
#> Permutation test with 10 relabelings of 6 levels of 'Patient' (paired design); smallest attainable p-value 1/10.
#> Refitting models ■■■■■■■■                          22% | ETA:  5s
#> Refitting models ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■                56% | ETA:  3s
#> Refitting models ■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■  100% | ETA:  0s
#>   Target Feature pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all    0.1      0.9304184

# p-values from the t-distribution: fast but anti-conservative
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    method = "t"
)
#>   Target Feature       pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all 3.051405e-05      0.9304184
